transcript.text: A commercial mission returning  cargo from the space station …
The first space station spacewalk of the year …
from space … a few of the stories to  tell you about – This Week at NASA!
A SpaceX Dragon cargo resupply spacecraft is  slated to return to Earth from the International
Space Station loaded with more than 4,900  pounds of cargo, including supplies and an
array of microgravity scientific experiments.  The Dragon’s return will cap off SpaceX’s 24th
Commercial Resupply Services mission for NASA.
the International Space Station to conduct  the station’s first spacewalk of the year.
During the outing, Anton Shkaplerov and Pyotr  Dubrov of Roscosmos performed work to prepare
the new Prichal docking module for future Russian  visiting spacecraft. The first docking to Prichal
is targeted for March, with the arrival of  three cosmonauts aboard a Soyuz spacecraft.
Several Earth-observing satellites are helping  scientists affiliated with NASA’s Disasters
programcollect and share data from the massive  volcanic eruption that obliterated the small,
uninhabited South Pacific island known as Hunga  Tonga-Hunga Ha‘apai. Damage assessments are
ongoing, but preliminary reports indicate that  populated communities in the island nation of
Tonga have taken heavy damage from volcanic  ash and a tsunami caused by the eruption.
Engineers at our Stennis Space Center conducted  the first RS-25 engine hot fire test of the
new year on Jan. 19. Four RS-25s will help  power our Space Launch System or (SLS) rocket
on future deep-space missions, including this  year’s uncrewed Artemis I mission around the Moon.
This was the second overall test in the current  test series which began in mid-December.
Each test provides valuable data that  can be used to help develop the engines.
The team assembling our X-59 Quiet SuperSonic  Technology (QueSST) aircraft is making great
progress with the developmental X-plane.  The crew successfully added the tail,
attached and tested out the positioning of  the nose, performed a system check of the
ejection seat, and moved the X-59’s  GE F414 engine to facilitate a 3D
engine scan. This scan helps engineers better  understand the F414’s fit in the engine bay.
The X-59 is being built to conduct research  aimed at reducing the loudness of sonic booms
that can occur during supersonic flight.
on these and other stories, follow  us on the web at nasa.gov/twan.
